text.en: Asha looked at a machine in a cloth mill. "Machines changed everything," said her teacher.

The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 18th century when hand production gave way to machines and factories. Inventions included the spinning jenny, the power loom and James Watt's steam engine.
Coal and iron fuelled industry, railways and steamships moved goods, and towns grew into cities. Factories needed workers, and many worked long hours in poor conditions, including children.
Industrial growth increased the demand for raw materials and markets, and led to colonies. It also brought new classes, labour movements and laws to protect workers.
The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 18th century when hand production gave way to machines and factories.
Inventions included the spinning jenny, the power loom and James Watt's steam engine.
Coal and iron fuelled industry, railways and steamships moved goods, and towns grew into cities.
Factories needed workers, and many worked long hours in poor conditions, including children.
Industrial growth increased the demand for raw materials and markets, and led to colonies.
It also brought new classes, labour movements and laws to protect workers.
Before the mid-eighteenth century, cloth, tools and shoes were made by hand in cottages—called the domestic system. The Industrial Revolution shifted production into power-driven factories.

Why did the Industrial Revolution start in Britain around 1760? Britain had rich coal and iron mines close together, navigable rivers and ports, a humid climate ideal for cotton spinning, and capital from overseas trade.

board.text: Why Britain? Coal, iron, ports & capital

text.en: Textiles led the breakthrough! John Kay's Flying Shuttle sped up weaving, James Hargreaves' Spinning Jenny spun multiple threads at once, and Richard Arkwright's Water Frame introduced water-powered mills.

board.text: Textile inventions: Flying Shuttle, Spinning Jenny, Water Frame

text.en: Samuel Crompton's Spinning Mule combined strength and fineness, and Edmund Cartwright's Power Loom mechanised weaving—multiplying cloth output hundreds of times.
In energy, James Watt dramatically improved the steam engine in 1769, freeing factories from riverbanks so mills could be built near coal fields and cities.
In metallurgy, Abraham Darby smelted iron with coke instead of charcoal, and later Henry Bessemer invented a fast process to turn iron into cheap, strong steel for bridges and rails.
Transport transformed next! John McAdam engineered smooth macadamised roads, canals linked mines to cities, and George Stephenson built the steam locomotive 'Rocket', launching the railway age.
Robert Fulton's steamboat sped up river and ocean travel, while Samuel Morse's electric telegraph and Alexander Graham Bell's telephone shrank communication across continents.
From Britain, industrialisation spread in the nineteenth century to France, Germany, Belgium, the United States and Meiji Japan, reshaping global power.
Industrialisation created rapid urbanisation: millions of rural villagers moved to factory towns like Manchester, Birmingham and Liverpool, which grew crowded and smoky.
Inside early factories, workers—including women and young children—endured fourteen-to-sixteen-hour days, dangerous unguarded machines, toxic coal dust and tiny wages.

board.text: Harsh early factory life & child labour

text.en: In response, workers formed trade unions to demand shorter hours and fair pay, and reformers passed Factory Acts banning young children from mines and limiting work hours.
New economic thinkers debated this world: Adam Smith advocated free markets (capitalism), while Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels criticised worker exploitation and proposed socialism.
Now look at the huge impact on India. Before 1750, Indian handloom weavers produced the finest muslin and calico exported worldwide.

board.text: Before 1750: India led world handloom textiles

text.en: Under British colonial rule, heavy tariffs blocked Indian cloth in Britain while cheap machine-made Lancashire textiles flooded India duty-free—causing severe deindustrialisation of Indian weavers.
India was turned from an exporter of finished cloth into a supplier of raw cotton, indigo and jute and a captive market for British factory goods.

Railways built by the British from 1853 onwards connected Indian ports to raw-material interiors, yet also unintentionally helped Indians travel, unite and build modern Indian industries like Tata Steel.
The Second Industrial Revolution in the late nineteenth century added electricity, internal combustion engines, chemicals and assembly-line mass production.
Environmental consequences began here too: massive coal burning filled industrial skies with smog and started the steady rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Yet industrialisation also brought lasting gains: affordable books, medicines, cleaner transport, wider education and higher living standards once labour laws protected workers.
Notice the chain of inventions: faster weaving created a yarn shortage -> better spinning machines -> steam power -> coal & iron -> railways to haul them all!
Compare two sides of the Industrial Revolution: technological triumph and higher output versus early worker hardship, child labour and colonial drain on India.

board.text: Two sides: progress vs human & colonial cost

text.en: Key names to remember: Hargreaves (Spinning Jenny), Watt (Steam Engine), Stephenson (Locomotive), Bessemer (Steel), Morse (Telegraph).
The Industrial Revolution built the modern machine age—teaching us that technological progress must always be paired with fair labour laws, equity and environmental care.

board.text: Technology must pair with fairness & care

problem.en: How did the Industrial Revolution in Britain affect India's traditional handloom weavers?

text.en: Compare India's status before and after 1800.

why.en: Before 1800, Indian handloom textiles were prized exports worldwide.

text.en: Identify the colonial trade policy.

why.en: Britain imposed high import duties on Indian cloth while letting cheap machine-made British textiles enter India nearly duty-free.

text.en: State the economic outcome.

why.en: Millions of Indian weavers lost their livelihoods—a process called deindustrialisation—while India became a raw-cotton supplier.
